audience: A designer shipping their first AI feature into a SaaS product, asking practical best-practice questions as they design it.
note: The asker has no visibility into the source documents at all — they are asking from their own situation, not referencing any file. Every answer is written as free-standing, actionable advice: no 'the document says', no file names, no 'per the source'. The internalSource field on each item is for whoever maintains this file only and is never shown to the asker.

questions.question: What accessibility standard should I be designing my AI chat feature against if I sell into Europe?
questions.answer: Treat WCAG 2.1 AA as your working baseline — it's folded into the current EU benchmark (EN 301 549 v3.2.1). A newer version that adds WCAG 2.2 has just been published but isn't formally in force yet, so build to 2.1 AA now and expect the bar to rise soon.

questions.question: Can I use an off-the-shelf accessibility overlay widget as a shortcut instead of fixing my AI feature's accessibility properly?
questions.answer: No, don't rely on one. Regulators have explicitly taken the position that these bolt-on widgets interfere with screen readers and other assistive tech rather than fixing anything, and they don't count toward compliance. Fix the interface itself.

questions.question: Should I give my AI feature broad access to our backend and APIs so it can do more for users, or keep it more limited?
questions.answer: Keep it more limited. Powerful, general-purpose access widens the range of ways the AI can go wrong, especially on unusual requests with no clean path to a solution. It's a reasonable trade to accept that the AI will sometimes refuse a request it can't safely handle, in exchange for keeping the damage it could ever do bounded. Design narrow, purpose-built actions rather than exposing raw power.

questions.question: How many tools or actions is too many to hand my AI assistant before it starts making more mistakes?
questions.answer: Raw count isn't really the driver — ambiguity is. A well-defined set of 15 or more distinct tools can work fine, while a confusing set of fewer than 10 can already cause problems. Spend your effort making each tool's purpose and inputs unambiguous rather than capping the number.

questions.question: Should I preload my AI feature with all of our product docs and data, or have it fetch what it needs on the fly?
questions.answer: Have it fetch on demand. Give it a search or lookup tool so it can pull in what a given task actually needs, rather than stuffing everything into its context up front. This keeps its answers grounded in what it actually looked at and avoids wasting effort on information most requests will never touch.

questions.question: What's a good pattern for handling 'what can you actually do?' questions without bloating my AI feature's main context?
questions.answer: Route that kind of question to a separate lookup step — a small dedicated call that searches your documentation in its own scratch space and returns just the answer. That keeps your main conversation lean instead of loading product docs into every single session.

questions.question: Should my AI feature ask for confirmation before every destructive action, or only in some cases?
questions.answer: Base it on consequence, not on which action is being taken. The same action can warrant a prompt in one situation and not in another — deleting something the AI itself just created a moment ago is lower-risk than deleting something that already existed before this session. Make as much as possible reversible, and reserve confirmation prompts for the genuinely irreversible cases.

questions.question: I'm planning to show a confirmation dialog before risky AI actions — will users actually keep reading it over time?
questions.answer: Assume not, after the first few times. Attention to a repeated warning drops fast — real-world data shows click-through rates as high as 70% for a familiar-looking warning, versus under 10% for one presented very differently. If a confirmation genuinely matters, make it look and behave differently enough each time that it forces real attention; otherwise expect it to get rubber-stamped.

questions.question: Should I build a live cost meter into my AI feature so users can see what each action is costing?
questions.answer: Only if it changes what they'd do. Ask yourself: after seeing this number, would the user act differently? If there's no clear answer, leave it out — a running cost meter is genuinely useful to whoever pays the bill (often an admin, not the end user), but for an everyday user it usually just adds worry with nothing to decide.

questions.question: Is a hard spending cap a good way to control AI costs in my product, or does it create its own problems?
questions.answer: It's worth having, but plan for the edge case: a cap that simply halts a job partway through can waste more than it saves, since the user has already paid for work they can't use yet. Give people a way to raise the limit and continue, rather than just hitting a dead stop.

questions.question: I added a workaround because our AI model kept losing track of tasks — do I need to plan to revisit that later?
questions.answer: Yes — write down why it exists and put a review date on it. Compensating mechanisms like this can turn harmful once the underlying model improves. A real example: a reminder mechanism that helped an early model stay on track later made an improved model stubbornly stick to a plan instead of adapting, and had to be swapped out for something built differently.

questions.question: When designing this feature, should I build for what the AI model can do today, or plan ahead for where it's headed?
questions.answer: Design roughly six months ahead of today's model, not for the exact one in front of you right now. Also keep a high bar for adding any new tool or affordance — each one is something you may eventually need to reconsider or remove as the model gets better.

questions.question: Do I need to disclose to my EU users that they're talking to an AI in my product, and what's the risk if I skip it?
questions.answer: Yes, this is a hard legal requirement for EU users, not just good practice, and it's on you even if you're using someone else's underlying model. Fines for skipping it can reach €15 million or 3% of global turnover.

questions.question: Can I satisfy that AI-disclosure requirement by putting a line about it in my terms of service or footer?
questions.answer: No, that's explicitly not enough. The notice needs to appear at the start of the conversation itself — burying it in terms of service, a footer, or a menu doesn't meet the bar.

questions.question: What's the best way to design my AI feature so it asks good clarifying questions instead of just guessing what the user wants?
questions.answer: Give it a dedicated, structured way to ask — a UI element that pauses the flow and presents two or three clear options with the trade-off stated for each, rather than trusting it to write a good question in plain prose. Bundling questions into an existing tool, or asking it to just output a specific text format, tends to be unreliable; a purpose-built blocking step works better.

questions.question: Should I let my AI feature ask as many follow-up questions as it wants before it starts the actual task?
questions.answer: No, cap it. A short, bounded round of clarifying questions (something like five, at most) before expensive work begins acts as a useful quality gate; an open-ended round starts to feel like an interrogation instead of a helpful check-in. Save the answers into whatever the AI produces next, rather than leaving them buried in the conversation.

questions.question: I'm evaluating a big list of AI UX patterns for my roadmap — what should I check about each one before adopting it?
questions.answer: Check five things: whether it's something to do, something to avoid, or something actively deceptive; what job it does in the interaction; what surface it lives on; how risky it is to get wrong; and how proven versus speculative it actually is. That last one matters most — treat anything unproven as a hypothesis to test with real users, not a settled answer.

questions.question: Before I commit to an approach, are there known unsolved problems in AI product design I should be aware of?
questions.answer: Yes, two worth flagging to your team: how one AI agent should hand off work to another cleanly, and whether trust actually carries over when a task moves from one AI to another. Nobody has a settled answer for either, so treat anything you build here as a first attempt, not a proven pattern.

questions.question: How do I design my AI feature so users can actually review and trust what it did, since my product isn't a coding tool?
questions.answer: Give the AI's output some reviewable, inspectable form — your own equivalent of a 'before and after' that a person can actually check. Coding tools get this for free from the diff; most other products don't, so manufacturing that reviewable artifact is itself a core design problem for you to solve. Anchor any feedback mechanism to the specific part of the output it concerns, since specific feedback gets a more precise correction than a general comment does.

questions.question: Can I promise my users an 'undo' button for whatever my AI feature does?
questions.answer: Only if your underlying system actually keeps a checkpoint to roll back to. Undo is an infrastructure capability before it's a UI affordance — check with engineering whether that checkpoint exists before you promise recoverability in the design.

questions.question: Instead of an approval dialog for every AI action, is there a better way to keep my feature bounded without wearing users out?
questions.answer: Consider a spending or scope cap the user sets once, instead of prompting per action. Per-action approval prompts reliably stop being read after repeated exposure, so a pre-agreed limit the AI works inside on its own is a more durable form of consent than a dialog nobody's actually reading by the third time.

questions.question: What EU compliance deadlines should be on my checklist before I launch this AI feature to European customers?
questions.answer: Two separate ones to track: telling users they're talking to an AI has been a live legal requirement since August 2026, with serious fines for skipping it. Separately, accessibility requirements for consumer products have been enforceable since mid-2025, with a stricter version of the standard recently published and headed toward formal adoption. Treat both as active requirements now, not upcoming ones.

questions.question: As I ship my first AI feature, what's the risk of the guardrails and workarounds I'm adding today?
questions.answer: They can quietly turn into constraints once the model improves. Guardrails built to cover for a model's current weaknesses — a scaffold that keeps it on-task, or a clumsy way of asking clarifying questions — often need replacing outright as capability improves, not just tuning. Write down why each guardrail exists and put it on a review schedule, rather than assuming today's fix is permanent.
